questions.question_text: Differentiate between real and virtual optical images.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: Real images are formed by actual intersecting rays and caught on screens. Virtual images are formed by apparent ray extensions and cannot be caught on screens.

questions.question_text: Explain how a concave parabolic mirror functions as a solar concentrator for cooking.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: A concave reflector reflects parallel incoming sunlight beams toward a single focal point. Concentrating solar radiation at this focal point generates intense thermal heat capable of cooking food.

questions.question_text: Describe image changes as an object moves from far away toward a concave mirror.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: 1. Object beyond C: Real, inverted, diminished image formed between F and C. 2. Object at C: Real, inverted image of equal size at C. 3. questions.question_text: Explain the principle of 10.1 Reflection Laws and Plane Mirrors and state its scientific significance.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: Light reflects according to two laws: 1. Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection (i = r). 2. Incident ray, reflected ray, and normal lie in the same plane. Plane mirrors form virtual, erect, laterally inverted images of equal size. [Think like a scientist: Real vs Virtual Images] Real images are formed by intersecting rays and caught on screens; virtual images cannot be caught on screens.

questions.question_text: Explain the principle of 10.2 Spherical Mirrors, Lenses, and Solar Applications and state its scientific significance.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: Concave mirrors converge light, forming real/inverted images (or virtual magnified images when close). Convex mirrors diverge light, forming diminished erect virtual images. Convex lenses magnify text. [Practical Application: Solar Concentrators] Large concave reflectors focus parallel sunlight to high thermal energy focal points.

questions.marking_scheme_answer: A concave parabolic mirror reflects incoming parallel sunlight beams toward a single point (focal point). Concentrating solar thermal radiation at this focus produces high temperatures capable of cooking food.
